metaDescription: We evaluated six lawn spreaders, push, pull-behind and handheld, on hopper size, spread width, tires, control and calibration to help you feed and seed evenly.
expertTake: The Scotts Turf Builder EdgeGuard DLX is our best overall pick because it covers up to 15,000 square feet per load, comes pre-calibrated and has a side-shield to keep product off beds and driveways. The Chapin TurfPro 100 lb is the value pick for bigger lawns. Anyone with a tiny yard should skip a push spreader and use a handheld, and owners of large lots should look at a pull-behind.
introParagraphs: A lawn spreader is the tool that decides whether fertiliser and grass seed land evenly or in stripes. Spread too thick and you burn the grass, too thin and you waste product and money, so even, repeatable flow is the whole point of the tool.

Most homeowners need a broadcast push spreader, which flings granules in a fan. Drop spreaders place product in a narrow band, handheld units suit small yards, and pull-behind models save time on larger lots. Hopper size, tire type and the quality of the gate control decide how it feels in use.

products.name: Scotts Turf Builder EdgeGuard DLX Broadcast Spreader

specList.label: Coverage per load
specList.value: Up to 15,000 square feet of Scotts product

products.description:
The Scotts EdgeGuard DLX is a walk-behind broadcast spreader that holds enough product for up to 15,000 square feet of Scotts lawn food, arrives pre-calibrated with no assembly, and uses a hopper with an agitator to keep granules flowing. The EdgeGuard feature lets you shut off the throw on one side so granules do not land on a driveway, flower bed or sidewalk, which matters because fertiliser on pavement can wash into storm drains.

The tradeoff is that the settings are tuned to Scotts products. If you use another brand of fertiliser or seed, you must look up the right setting and test it, because the printed numbers will not match. Compared with the Chapin TurfPro, which has a bigger hopper and a slide-adjust gate, the Scotts is lighter and simpler but needs refilling sooner on a large lawn. It suits typical suburban lawns up to a third of an acre.

Ownership centres on cleaning. Empty the hopper after each use, rinse the unit, and let it dry fully so fertiliser salts do not corrode the metal parts. Check the tires and gate for stiffness, store it dry, and lubricate the gate hinge once a season.
products.bestFor: Typical suburban lawns where simple, calibrated spreading and edge control matter.
pros: Arrives pre-calibrated with no assembly required
EdgeGuard blocks the throw on one side near beds and driveways
Fifteen thousand square feet per load limits refills
Works for seed, fertiliser, salt and ice melt year-round
cons: Printed settings are tuned to Scotts products, not other brands
Needs refilling more often than 100 lb commercial models

products.name: CHAPIN TurfPro 100 lb Push Lawn Spreader
products.description:
The Chapin TurfPro is a push spreader with a 100 pound hopper that the listing says covers up to 22,000 square feet, a slide-adjust lever for the gate opening and a large T-shaped handle with rubber grips. It is aimed at contractors and homeowners with larger yards who want fewer refills.

The tradeoff is weight and calibration. A full 100 pounds of fertiliser is heavy to push, and a slide gate gives you a continuous range of settings rather than printed numbers, so you must test your flow rate with a measured area. Compared with the Scotts EdgeGuard DLX, the Chapin has more capacity but no edge shield, so you must steer carefully near beds. It suits half-acre lawns and anyone who spreads often.

Rinse the hopper and gate after each use, dry the metal parts, and oil the slide lever. Check the tires and axle for wear, and store the unit with the hopper empty.
products.bestFor: Larger lawns where fewer refills outweigh the extra weight.
pros: One hundred pound hopper covers up to 22,000 square feet
Slide-adjust lever allows fine control of the gate opening
Large T-handle with rubber grips is comfortable for long passes
Suits contractor and residential use alike
cons: Heavy to push when the hopper is full
No edge shield, so you must steer carefully near beds

products.name: EarthWay 2150 Commercial 50 lb Broadcast Spreader
products.description:
The EarthWay 2150 is a heavy-duty walk-behind broadcast spreader with 13 inch pneumatic stud tires on rustproof poly rims, a clog-free grate that screens out lumps and a 3-hole drop system with side-spread control for a feathered edge. The big tires roll over rough, uneven ground without bouncing granules out, and the 50 pound hopper is a sensible size to push.

The tradeoff is cost and hopper size. A 50 pound hopper covers less ground per load than the 100 pound Chapin, so large lawns need more refills, and air-filled tires can go flat. Compared with the Scotts EdgeGuard DLX, the EarthWay is built to a more durable, commercial standard with a better ride on bumps. It suits owners with rough or sloping lawns and anyone who spreads often.

Rinse and dry the spreader after use, check tire pressure, and lubricate the gate and gears. Replace the grate if it bends, since a damaged grate lets lumps clog the holes.
products.bestFor: Uneven or rough lawns where tire size and build quality matter.
pros: Thirteen inch pneumatic tires roll smoothly over bumps
Clog-free grate screens out lumps before they block the holes
Three-hole drop with side-spread control feathers the edges
Rustproof poly rims resist corrosion from fertiliser salts
cons: Fifty pound hopper means more refills on large lawns
Air tires can lose pressure and need checking

products.name: Agri-Fab 130 lb Pull-Behind Broadcast Spreader

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Up to 25,000 square feet, about half an acre

products.description:
The Agri-Fab is a pull-behind spreader with a 130 pound hopper, a listed coverage of up to half an acre per load and a spread width of 10 to 12 feet. A universal hitch connects it to most riding mowers and lawn tractors, so the engine does the walking while you steer.

The tradeoff is that you need a tractor or large mower, and a wide spread is harder to keep even near edges. Compared with a push spreader like the Chapin, the Agri-Fab covers far more ground per hour, but it is less precise around beds and takes more storage space. It suits properties over half an acre where a push spreader would take a morning.

Rinse the hopper after each use, grease the axle, and check the tires and hitch pin. Keep the gate and agitator clean, and store it dry.
products.bestFor: Large lawns of half an acre or more where you already own a riding mower.
pros: One hundred thirty pound hopper covers up to half an acre
Universal hitch fits most riding mowers and tractors
Ten to twelve foot spread cuts passes dramatically
Saves hours compared with a push spreader on large lawns
cons: Requires a tractor or riding mower to tow it
Wide throw is less precise near beds and edges

products.name: Amazon Basics Broadcast Spreader, 5,000 Sq Ft per Load
products.description:
The Amazon Basics spreader is a small broadcast model that the listing rates for up to 5,000 square feet per load, with a multi-gear system for precision control. It handles seed, fertiliser, salt and ice melt, and is sized for small to medium yards.

The tradeoff is capacity and refinement. A 5,000 square foot hopper means a few refills on anything bigger than a small lawn, and a basic build gives you fewer features than the Scotts or EarthWay. Compared with the Scotts EdgeGuard DLX, it costs less but lacks the edge shield and the pre-calibrated setting tied to a known product. It suits small yards and occasional users.

Rinse and dry after use, check the gears for grit, and lubricate lightly. Replace the unit if the gate sticks or the gears strip.
products.bestFor: Small yards where an occasional-use spreader at a gentle tier is enough.
pros: Small footprint is easy to store in a shed or garage
Multi-gear operation gives some control over flow
Handles seed, fertiliser, salt and ice melt
Sized for a typical small yard
cons: Five thousand square feet per load means frequent refills
Fewer features than premium homeowner models

products.name: Scotts Whirl Hand-Powered Spreader

specList.label: Coverage per load
specList.value: Up to 1,500 square feet of Scotts product

products.description:
The Scotts Whirl is a hand-cranked spreader with an adjustable arm support, a listed capacity of up to 1,500 square feet of Scotts product and a design aimed at small yards. You hold it against your hip, turn the crank and the spinner flings granules, which is handy for patchy repairs, small lawns and spreading ice melt on steps.

The tradeoff is speed and evenness. A handheld unit covers less area per fill and relies on a steady walking pace and crank speed to keep the spread even, so a push spreader gives better consistency. Compared with the Amazon Basics push model, the Whirl is smaller and cheaper to store, but it is tiring on anything larger than a small lawn. It suits spot seeding and tight spaces.

Rinse the hopper, dry it thoroughly and keep the crank gears clean. Store it empty so leftover fertiliser does not cake.
products.bestFor: Small yards, spot seeding and spreading salt on steps.
pros: Compact handheld size is easy to store and carry
Adjustable arm support improves comfort
Useful for patches, edges and tight spaces
Handles seed, fertiliser, salt and ice melt
cons: Even spreading depends on steady walking and cranking pace
Too tiring and slow for anything above a small lawn

buyingCriteria.explanation: Broadcast spreaders fling granules in a fan and cover more ground quickly, drop spreaders place a narrow band and give precision near edges, and handhelds suit small jobs. Most lawns suit a broadcast push spreader like the Scotts or Chapin. Choose a drop spreader only if you often feed a lawn that borders beds and want zero overspray.

Capacity decides how often you refill. The Amazon Basics covers about 5,000 square feet per load, the Scotts about 15,000, the Chapin about 22,000 and the Agri-Fab about 25,000. Remember these are product-dependent estimates, so a heavy seed uses more per area than a light fertiliser.

Even spreading depends on a repeatable gate setting. Pre-calibrated settings like the Scotts are easiest if you use the same brand. Slide-adjust gates, as on the Chapin, are flexible but need testing. Always test your flow over a measured area, because printed numbers are only a starting point.

Small plastic wheels bounce on rough lawns and throw an uneven pattern. Large pneumatic tires, like the 13 inch ones on the EarthWay, roll smoothly over bumps. If you have a sloping or lumpy lawn, tire size matters more than hopper size.

Spread width tells you how wide the throw is, from about 8 feet on small units to 12 feet on pull-behinds. Wider is faster but harder to control near edges. An edge shield, as on the Scotts EdgeGuard, protects beds and pavement and reduces runoff.

Fertiliser is corrosive, so powder-coated steel, stainless parts and poly rims last longer. Cheap bare steel gates rust shut. The EarthWay uses rustproof poly rims, and the Scotts uses plastic parts that shrug off salts. Always rinse and dry after use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared hopper size and the coverage figures the makers state. The Agri-Fab and Chapin lead on capacity, and the Amazon Basics trails. We treated coverage claims as product-dependent estimates.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spread control and calibration
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at gate design, calibration and edge features from published specifications. The Scotts is pre-calibrated and has EdgeGuard, while the Chapin uses a slide lever. Spreaders without edge control were noted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wheels and terrain handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We researched tire size and type, using owner feedback patterns on rough lawns. Large pneumatic tires, like the EarthWay's, scored well. Small plastic wheels were noted for bounce.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and corrosion resistance
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered frame materials, gate parts and rims. Rustproof poly rims and powder-coated steel earned credit. Bare steel gates were flagged as a corrosion risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for lawn size
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each spreader to lawn sizes from small yards to half an acre. A handheld suits a small yard, a push spreader suits most homes, and a pull-behind suits large lots. We judged value by fit.

maintenance.why: Fertiliser salts corrode metal and clog the gate. A quick rinse prevents both.
Trapped moisture rusts steel parts and cakes leftover granules. Let it air dry before storing.
Dry gates stick and gears wear. A light lubricant keeps the control smooth.
Low pressure or a loose axle gives an uneven spread. Inflate and tighten as needed.

maintenance.interval: At the start of the season
maintenance.why: Settings drift with product and wear. A test patch confirms you are applying the right rate.

faq.q: Is a broadcast spreader better than a drop spreader?
faq.a: For most lawns, yes, because a broadcast spreader covers more ground and blends overlaps. A drop spreader is better when you need exact placement near beds and edges, but it takes more passes.

faq.q: How much should I spend on a lawn spreader?
faq.a: A handheld costs little, a homeowner push model costs more, and a commercial or pull-behind model costs the most. Spend for capacity and tires if your lawn is large or rough.

faq.q: How long does a lawn spreader last?
faq.a: A well-rinsed spreader can last many years. Corrosion of the gate and gears is the usual failure, so rinse and dry after every use.

faq.q: Do the printed settings work for any fertiliser?
faq.a: No. Printed settings are tuned to a specific product, so other brands need testing. Check the bag for the manufacturer's spreader setting and test over a measured patch.

faq.q: Is it safe to spread near children and pets?
faq.a: Follow the product label, since some fertilisers and weed killers need the lawn to stay clear until watered in or dry. Keep people and pets off the area for the time the label states.

faq.q: Can I use a lawn spreader for ice melt?
faq.a: Yes, most can, but rinse thoroughly afterwards because salt corrodes metal quickly. A dedicated cheap handheld for salt protects your main spreader.
